source.title: Light Chemical Elements in Stars: Mysteries and Unsolved Problems

accepted.question_text: Why is the primordial lithium abundance inferred from old FGK dwarf stars in the Galactic halo, with log ε(7Li) ≈ 2.2 on the Spite plateau, lower by about 0.5 dex than the Standard Model of the Big Bang prediction of about 2.7, even though the same model agrees well with observed primordial abundances of deuterium, 3He, and 4He?

evidence.quote: Despite repeated attempts to solve the problem of the lithium abundance in old stars of the galactic halo, as before two important questions remain as mysteries for the theory: (1) why is there a discrepancy of 0.5 dex between the observed lithium abundance and the primordial abundance predicted by the SMBB?

accepted.question_text: Why do a significant fraction of old FGK dwarf stars in the Galactic halo have lithium abundances substantially below the Spite plateau at log ε(Li) ≈ 2.2, rather than clustering near that plateau value?

evidence.quote: (2) why do a significant fraction of the halo dwarfs have a lithium abundance significantly below the "lithium plateau?"

accepted.question_text: What physical mechanism can explain the observed helium enrichment of early B-type main-sequence stellar atmospheres, especially for stars of about 12–19 solar masses where He/H increases by more than a factor of two toward the end of the main-sequence stage, even though most such stars have relatively low rotation velocities and current rotating-star models predict much smaller helium enhancement?

evidence.quote: Thus, there are some serious disagreements between the theory and the observations. The observational data on the increased helium abundance in the atmospheres of early B-type MS stars suggest that the theoretical models seriously underestimate the abundance of helium (the main product of the CNO-cycle) transported to the surface of a star by mixing.
Therefore, explaining the observed helium enrichment of the atmosphere of early B-type MS stars is still an unsolved problem for the theory.

accepted.question_text: Why do early B- and O-type stars that are components of close binary systems retain their original low helium abundance through roughly the first half of the main-sequence stage and then undergo a sharp increase in He/H by about a factor of two over the short interval t/tMS ≈ 0.5–0.7, and how should stellar mixing models incorporate both rotation and tidal interaction effects to reproduce this behavior?

evidence.quote: Figure 5 shows that, as opposed to the gradual, monotonic increase in He/H observed in isolated hot stars (Figs. 3 and 4), the low (original) helium abundance is retained in the components of close binary systems throughout the first half of their evolution on the Main Sequence (t/tMS<0.5). Then, over the short interval of t/tMS from 0.5 to 0.7, there is a sharp increase in He/H by roughly a factor of two, after which He/H remains at this higher level until the end of the MS stage.

For the modern theory this kind of sudden rise in He/H in the atmosphere in the middle of the MS stage is a mystery. Calculations of mixing in the MS are needed both for isolated stars and for the components of close binary systems where, besides rotation, the tidal interactions of the components must be taken into account.

accepted.question_text: Why are three different kinds of B-type main-sequence stars found in the same effective-temperature range of about 17000–25000 K—He-strong stars with enhanced helium, He-weak stars with depleted helium, and chemically normal B-type stars—and what mechanism determines which helium-abundance class a given star occupies?

evidence.quote: It is interesting that for Teff between 17000 and 25000 K, three different types of B-type MS stars are observed in the Main Sequence stage: He-s, He-w, and normal B-type MS stars. This phenomenon is one of the unsolved problems for CP-type stars.

accepted.question_text: Can a quantitative diffusion-based model for chemically peculiar main-sequence stars simultaneously explain the helium and lithium anomalies together with the broader abundance pattern, including the tendency for element excesses to grow with atomic number, the surface spot distribution of different elements, and the depth-dependent stratification of abundances within a single star?

evidence.quote: A diffusion hypothesis has been proposed as the basic explanation for these features of the composition of CP-stars. This means that these features are not associated with thermonuclear processes in the interior of a star, but are a result of the diffusion of atoms in its surface layers under the influence of two oppositely directed forces—gravitation and radiation pressure. In magnetic CP-stars, the magnetic field also contributes.

Detailed calculations of diffusion for any specific CP-star which might provide a quantitative explanation for all the observed phenomena, including the general trend toward excesses of all the observed elements with increasing Z, a map of the distribution of spots of different elements over the surface of a star, and the distributions of different elements with depth, are a difficult problem. It has not yet been solved completely for any individual CP-star.

accepted.question_text: What theoretical mechanism can reproduce, for FGK dwarf stars in old clusters such as the Hyades, both the overall decrease of lithium, beryllium, and boron abundances with falling effective temperature and the pronounced abundance dip near Teff ≈ 6600 K, including the different dip depths observed for Li, Be, and B?

evidence.quote: The problems discussed above might be regarded as solved if some model calculations could reproduce the observed distributions of the abundances of Li, Be, and B with respect to Teff, e.g., for the stars in the Hyades (as in Fig. 6). No such calculations, however, have yet been done.

Therefore, the reduction in the abundances of lithium and beryllium in the atmospheres of FGK-dwarfs (including the sun, where Li is reduced by a factor of 140), as well as the trend with Teff and the dip in the abundances of Li, Be, and B in stars in old clusters such as the Hyades, still have no theoretical solution.

accepted.question_text: How are lithium-rich and super-lithium-rich FGK giants and supergiants produced when many of these stars cannot be explained by standard stellar-evolution theory, some have already passed through deep convective mixing that should have destroyed their surface lithium, and candidate mechanisms such as post-mixing lithium synthesis through the Cameron–Fowler process, extra mixing, or engulfment of a giant planet do not yet provide a complete explanation?

evidence.quote: Giants and supergiants that are rich in lithium (with    2Lilog ) are of heightened interest since most of them cannot be explained in terms of the standard theory of stellar evolution.
The remaining Li-rich giants and all the super Li-rich giants are completely unexplainable in terms of the standard theory of stellar evolution.
There are two competing hypotheses for explaining stars that are rich in lithium. The first is recent synthesis of lithium after a DCM by the Cameron-Fowler mechanism [37].
The second hypothesis is capture of a giant planet with mass equal to that of Jupiter or more by the star.

accepted.question_text: Why do the cold supergiants HR 461 and HR 8313, which are more massive than about 6 solar masses, still show detectable lithium even though stellar-evolution calculations predict that stars in this mass range should have destroyed essentially all atmospheric lithium before reaching the red-giant or supergiant phase?

evidence.quote: Thus, in all stars with  6 MM  practically all the lithium should burn up, even before their entry into the red giant/supergiant phase. Figure 7 shows that two stars in this group, the supergiants HR 461 (K0 Ia) and HR 8313 (G5 Ib) for which lithium has been detected at a level of   .~ 51Lilog , are in conflict with this theory.

accepted.question_text: How can atmospheric models of early B-type and late O-type stars be improved so that they correctly account for the superionization of C II, N II, and O II, avoid the systematic discrepancy between temperatures and gravities derived from ionization-balance methods versus traditional photometric and Balmer-line methods, and thereby yield reliable carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen abundances?

evidence.quote: But another problem shows up: a systematic discrepancy between the values of Teff and logg found by fundamentally different methods.

In order to solve the superionization problem for hot stars to study the abundances of C, N, and O in their atmospheres, it is necessary to shift to more realistic models of their atmospheres: this assumes a transition from plane-parallel models to spherical models, as well as including stellar wind and the magnetic field that has been observed in a number of O- and B-type stars.
